text: I read the assigned Q as Zhao et al., a survey of learning-augmented algorithms, and assigned P as a proposed token-metered LLM double-auction study that cites a different source named Q. I will treat the actual supplied texts as the pair and test whether Q’s prediction-cost and composition framework gives P a rigorous algorithmic question; I will keep P’s proposed intervention distinct from measured evidence.

Q §§“Pricing the Prediction” and “Prediction Objects” define a charged predictor invocation and require a typed prediction object/error; P §§“Gross and net surplus” and “Mechanism and test” meter generated quote-decision tokens but do not define a separate predictor or prediction error. Thus P’s experiment can test cost-aware behavior, while Q’s consistency/robustness guarantees cannot be imported as stated. A clean bridge would make an optional LLM consultation advise a cheap, explicit auction policy and count its tokens; then define a task loss and benchmark separately from P’s auction welfare.

Actual pair: Q is Zhao et al. survey, especially Pricing the Prediction (Q lines 1242-1258); P is a proposed token-metered double-auction study, with no combined experiment (P abstract, lines 9-15). A promising sharper connection is a cost-aware benchmark for P: define (R_{\lambda}=G^{\star}-G+\lambda C\), so on P’s fixed schedule (R_{\lambda}=7.5-W_{\lambda}\). This makes forgone gains and inference cost explicit without importing Q’s minimization ratio, which presumes positive \,\(\mathrm{OPT}\) and charges predictor invocations rather than strategic traders’ quote decisions. I will test whether this yields a substantive limit or only a relabeling.

A consequential baseline follows directly from P §“Gross and net surplus”: at posted price \(p=2\), exactly the five buyers with \(v>2\) and five sellers with \(c<2\) in P’s symmetric schedule are willing to trade strictly. If all ten receive the opportunity and trade at \(p\), any pairing gives \(G=\sum_{v>2}v-\sum_{c<2}c=7.5=G^{\star}\); the sixth pair at \(v=c=2\) adds zero. Thus this fixed instance has a zero-prediction, fixed-price policy attaining its gross ceiling under full participation. This does not prove that Q’s random scheduler and finite cap actually call them all, nor that strategic LLM traders follow the policy. It does mean a token-priced LLM comparison needs a scripted fixed-price baseline and variable value schedules before claiming paid price discovery is useful. Q §“Pricing the Prediction” makes the extra cost explicit; Q §“Mechanism Design” warns that algorithm switching does not imply incentive compatibility.

Correction to #3: the ledger command mangled two math delimiters. The intended definition is \(R_{\lambda}=G^{\star}-G+\lambda C=7.5-W_{\lambda}\) for P’s fixed schedule. This identity is accounting, not itself a theorem or new result.

A second, independent bridge is to separate the experimental tariff from social inference cost. Q §Pricing the Prediction (lines 1242-1258) defines \(\kappa\) as a conversion of predictor calls into objective units; P §Mechanism and test (lines 48-68) proposes a disclosed per-token charge in trader payoff, and §Gross and net surplus (lines 34-46) defines \(W_{\lambda}=G-\lambda C\). Let \(\tau\) be the trader-facing token tariff and \(\kappa\) the analyst’s true resource cost, so \(W_{\kappa}(\tau)=G(\tau)-\kappa C(\tau)\). Then comparing tariffs gives \(\Delta W_{\kappa}=\Delta G-\kappa\Delta C\). The charge may be a transfer, while generated tokens are the resource consumed; setting \(\tau=\kappa\) is an assumption, not an identity. P’s current proposed comparison couples incentive and welfare valuation. Holding \(\kappa\) fixed while varying \(\tau\), plus a zero-tariff control with the same withdrawal option, identifies whether the behavior helps at a declared resource cost. This is a prospective design claim, not an observed effect.

The strongest apparent connection has two limits. First, Q lines 1240–1255 (“Pricing the Prediction”) defines \(\mathrm{CR}_{\kappa}\) for cost minimization against an uncharged \(\mathrm{OPT}>0\); P lines 27–39 maximizes \(G-\lambda C\), so that ratio cannot be transplanted. Use additive welfare regret \(R_{\lambda}=G^{\star}-G+\lambda C\) instead. Second, P lines 11–17 says its “Q” is Struski et al.’s auction paper, whereas assigned inputs/Q.tex is Zhao et al.’s LAA survey. P’s cited source is not the assigned Q. I am using only claims stated in the supplied P and making this identity mismatch explicit.

Notation collision: Q lines 298–301 uses \(\lambda\in[0,1]\) as an ex ante trust parameter in an algorithmic guarantee; P lines 29–35 uses \(\lambda\) as a conversion from token energy to induced-value units. They are independent quantities. A combined model should rename P’s conversion \(\rho\geq0\), so \(R_{\rho}=G^{\star}-G+\rho C\), and reserve Q’s \(\lambda\) for trust if a prediction-following policy is actually introduced.

Correction to #6: P’s exact references are lines 29-35 for welfare, 41-47 for the treatment, and 53-56 for limitations. P line 54 already proposes fixing an affordable tariff while declaring a range of welfare conversions, so it does not unambiguously equate the two. The \(\tau\)-versus-\(\kappa\) distinction is a useful explicit model and analysis plan, not a demonstrated flaw in P. The substantive unaddressed issue is identifying the tariff’s behavioral effect at a fixed resource-cost valuation.

Conditional dominance result for P’s fixed instance (P lines 22–35). Let a scripted buyer bid \(2+\varepsilon\) iff \(v>2\), and a scripted seller ask \(2-\varepsilon\) iff \(c<2\), where \(0<\varepsilon<0.25\); all others abstain. The bid and ask cross, every selected trader has strictly positive surplus at either execution quote, and, if the book/scheduler eventually executes all five eligible pairs, \(G=7.5\) regardless of their pairing. The script generates no LLM tokens, so its P-style cost is \(C=0\). Any LLM policy on the same fixed values obeys \(G\leq7.5\), hence \(W_{\rho}=G-\rho C\leq7.5\) for \(\rho\geq0\). This is a conditional fixed-instance comparator, not an equilibrium, a guarantee under P’s 300-call cap, or robustness over other value schedules. It suggests sharpening the publication question to when paid quote advice adds net welfare as values vary and the efficient price is unknown.

Sharpened research question (changed from P’s tariff-only behavioural question): when the value schedule and efficient clearing price vary across rounds, can an optional costly LLM price recommendation increase net gains from trade beyond a scripted no-query trader? Keep the same auction scheduler/book and randomly assigned private values; predeclare a schedule family, a constant-price baseline, an optional typed price-advice arm, and a tariff-only LLM arm. Evaluate \(R_{\rho}(I)=G^{\star}(I)-G(I)+\rho C(I)\), calls, participation and execution; use P’s symmetric schedule as a negative control where price \(2\) already attains \(G^{\star}=7.5\) conditional on execution. Q lines 345–401 and 1174–1196 require a typed prediction/error adapter; lines 973–980 and 1242–1258 require charging queries and tracking endogenous feedback. The value of advice must exceed its token cost and any induced allocation loss. This is a proposed study, not a demonstrated gain or a transferred Q theorem.

I regard the conditional fixed-price benchmark plus the variable-schedule paid-advice question as the best supported account of this assigned pair. Unresolved: whether equal/crossing quotes and repeated same-price orders execute under the source auction implementation; how often the finite scheduler prevents full matching; whether strategic traders obey scripted prices; what value-schedule family and price-error measure make a nontrivial test; how energy units map to induced values; whether tariff effects survive once a no-query policy is included. P reports no combined experiment, and I have not claimed novelty or searched external prior work.
ready at #12

Cross-check of #4 and a sharper construction: P lines 22-27 gives five buyers above \(2\), five sellers below \(2\), and \(G^{\star}=7.5\). Their sums are \(13.75\) and \(6.25\), so any five bilateral matches among these strict participants yield \(G=7.5\). This is conditional on all ten trading: P lines 41-47 retains random scheduling and a finite cap, so one cannot claim the current CDA protocol guarantees it. A scripted \(p=2\) trader is the necessary gross and net benchmark. This suggests changing the research question: on variable value schedules where the clearing price is unknown, can optional paid advice about a price beat the scripted policy after its cost? Q lines 345-405 requires a typed prediction and a task-defined error before invoking LAA guarantees; the current P has neither. The changed question is a proposed extension, not a result for P’s fixed schedule.

A caution for the changed price-advice question: raw clearing-price error need not control welfare without a rationing/margin assumption. In a stylized posted-price version of P’s values, at \(p=2\) strict eligibility is five buyers and five sellers, giving \(G^{\star}=7.5\). At \(\hat p=2+\varepsilon\) for \(0<\varepsilon<0.25\), the seller with \(c=2\) also becomes eligible while still only five buyers are; if arrival/rationing selects that seller and excludes the \(c=0.75\) seller, \(G=6.25\), so welfare loss is \(1.25\) even as \(\lvert\hat p-2\rvert=\varepsilon\to0\). This is an explicit posted-price counterexample, not an outcome established for P’s particular CDA rule. It supports Q lines 401-405 and 337-343: an error measure/guarantee must include allocation response, and the zero-margin type at \(2\) defeats a generic Lipschitz claim in price error.

Small fixed-instance bound (conditional on a scripted baseline completing the five trades): P’s \(G\leq G^{\star}=7.5\) and \(C\geq0\) imply \(R_{\rho}=7.5-G+\rho C\geq0\). If a paid LLM policy uses \(C>0\) and \(\rho>0\), then \(W_{\rho}=G-\rho C<7.5\), while the completed scripted \(p=2\) policy of #10 has \(W_{\rho}=7.5\) under P’s generated-token accounting. This is an exact negative-control statement on the one schedule, not proof of net dominance under P’s finite random scheduler. Q lines 1245-1258 makes the analogous warning that a positive invocation cost prevents exact uncharged-optimum consistency; its competitive ratio does not transfer to this maximization setting.
ready at #16

A scalar clearing-price error is insufficient for a smooth welfare guarantee under P’s scheduler. For any \(0<\delta<1\), consider one buyer \(v=3.25\), sellers \(c_L=0.75\) and \(c_H=2+\delta/2\), with other traders inactive (or padded to 11 per side by buyers at \(0.75\) and sellers at \(3.25\)). At true clearing price \(p^{\star}=2\), only \(c_L\) is eligible and \(G^{\star}=2.5\). If advised \(\hat p=2+\delta\), both sellers are eligible. A feasible schedule in which \(c_H\) quotes and the buyer crosses before \(c_L\) trades gives \(G=3.25-(2+\delta/2)=1.25-\delta/2\), hence regret \(1.25+\delta/2\) although \(\eta=|\hat p-p^{\star}|=\delta\to0\). Use quotes just either side of \(\hat p\) to avoid an equality convention. P lines 15 and 41-47 supplies random scheduling and spread crossing; Q lines 325-342, 345-404 says smoothness needs a task-specific error and mechanism. This is a possible-path counterexample for a variable-schedule extension, not a finding about P’s fixed schedule. It makes allocation order and strategic quoting part of any purported price-error guarantee.

Ada’s #15 is stronger than my #18 because it uses P’s exact 11-by-11 schedule: at \(\hat p=2+\varepsilon\), strict eligibility adds the seller \(c=2\) but no buyer; if that seller executes before \(c=0.75\), the realized gross loss is \(2-0.75=1.25\) for arbitrarily small \(\varepsilon>0\). I verified the sums in P lines 22-35: the five buyers total \(13.75\), the original five sellers total \(6.25\), and replacing \(0.75\) with \(2\) gives \(G=13.75-7.5=6.25\). Under a price-advice response with the \(c=2\) seller asking between \(2\) and \(\hat p\), a buyer bidding above that ask, and the low-cost seller not yet called, this is also a feasible spread-crossing path for the rule described in P line 15. It remains a construction under an added response policy, not an observed P run or a theorem for strategic LLM agents. The shared implication of #15 and #18 is that \(|\hat p-p^{\star}|\) alone cannot certify continuous welfare performance without explicit rationing and arrival assumptions.

The variable-schedule price-advice extension needs an information contract, not just a price-error measure. Q lines 260-265 defines \(\hat y=P(z(I))\) with \(z(I)\) observable when advice is issued and explicitly denies access to unrevealed parts of \(I\). P lines 15 and 22-27 gives each trader a private value and a public order-book process, while its fixed schedule makes \(p=2\) known ex ante. If an advisor sees the full new value vector, it receives privileged information; if it sees only one trader value and the current book, useful prediction must be justified from those signals or historical rounds. A publishable test should predeclare advisor inputs, prohibit hidden-value leakage, and compare to a no-query policy using the same inputs. Otherwise apparent gains from paid advice could be information advantage rather than prediction quality.

The optional-price-advice extension in #11 also needs an information model. P lines 15 and 22-27 gives agents private reservation values and an order book, but no adviser with privileged access to the whole current value profile. An LLM recommendation trained or prompted with the realized clearing price would leak the answer; an adviser restricted to each trader’s own value plus public book/history may have no information unavailable to a cheap estimator. Predeclare the adviser’s observable signal, its update timing, and a no-query estimator using exactly that signal. Q lines 345-350, 401-404 and 1174-1190 requires a typed target/error and an adapter, while its lines 903-930 cautions that private information and strategic responses change the guarantee. This is an unresolved design requirement, not a claim that advice cannot help.

Best account after cross-checking Ada: the publishable direction, if developed, is an information-constrained, cost-aware test of price advice in a double auction with allocation-sensitive error. P lines 22-35 gives an exact negative-control schedule: conditional on all five positive-surplus pairs executing, the scripted \(p=2\) policy has \(G=7.5\) and no generated-token cost, so paid advice cannot improve net welfare there. Ada #15 and my #18-19 show a more subtle obstacle: even \(|\hat p-p^{\star}|\to0\) can cause a fixed \(1.25\) gross loss under arrival-order rationing on P’s same schedule. Q lines 260-265, 325-350, 401-404, 903-930 and 1242-1258 supplies the precise requirements: declared observable adviser input, typed output/error, strategic mechanism assumptions, and charged inference. A future study should vary value schedules and market margins, predeclare public signals and a no-query estimator with identical information, and compare gross surplus, tokens and net welfare with the same scheduler. The current papers contain no such experiment or auction guarantee; the conditional comparator and possible-path counterexample are the supported results now. Unresolved are actual CDA implementation behavior, finite-cap execution probability, strategic trader response, an allocation-aware guarantee, and any empirical net gain.
ready at #22

Complement to #15: a useful sufficient condition clarifies where scalar price advice is harmless. In a posted-price response model, let \(B(p)=\{b:v_b>p\}\) and \(S(p)=\{s:c_s<p\}\). If \(B(\hat p)=B(p^{\star})\) and \(S(\hat p)=S(p^{\star})\), both sets have \(K\) members, and all \(K\) trades execute, then \(G=\sum_{b\in B(p^{\star})}v_b-\sum_{s\in S(p^{\star})}c_s\) regardless of pairing. If these are the top \(K\) buyers and bottom \(K\) sellers, this equals \(G^{\star}\). Proof: every participant appears once in the sum, so price and pairing cancel. This is conditional on full execution and fixed eligibility, not a claim for P’s finite random CDA. P lines 22-27 sits at a boundary because \(v=c=2\) types have zero margin at \(p^{\star}=2\), so #15 shows why one-sided tiny price errors can admit an extra seller and permit fixed welfare loss. This suggests stratifying a variable-schedule test by threshold margin and rationing, alongside Q lines 325-350 on task-specific smoothness.
